title: Better at shooting left. Shoot left more?
hook: A kicker improves one side. Should he use it more often?

knows: a goalkeeper must guess a side before the kick
a probability such as 0.9 means 9 times in 10
doesNotKnow: that in a mixed equilibrium your mix is set by what makes the other side indifferent
that improving your own weapon can make you use it less

misconception: If I get better at shooting left, I should shoot left more.
objective: The learner can say that when the kicker's left shot improves, the keeper must cover the left more, so the kicker's best mix shoots left less even though his overall scoring chance rises.

claims.text: In the toy game (the kicker scores 0.5 when the keeper dives the way the ball goes, 0.9 on a kick to the right when the keeper dives left, and 0.9 or 1.0 on a kick to the left when the keeper dives right), the kicker's best mix shoots left 50.0% of the time at 0.90 and 44.4% at 1.00.
claims.source: Kicker left-share p makes the keeper indifferent: p*0.5 + (1-p)*0.9 = p*x + (1-p)*0.5, so p = (0.9-0.5)/((x-0.5)+(0.9-0.5)). x=0.90: 0.4/0.8 = 0.500. x=1.00: 0.4/0.9 = 0.4444. Re-run in node with Demo.tsx mix(); the six slider states give 0.500, 0.488, 0.476, 0.465, 0.455, 0.444. Revised v3: claim text reworded per fact-check pass NCM-1 (dive direction by kick).

claims.text: In the same game the keeper's best mix dives left 50.0% of the time at 0.90 and 55.6% at 1.00.
claims.source: Keeper left-share q makes the kicker indifferent: q*0.5 + (1-q)*x = q*0.9 + (1-q)*0.5, so q = (x-0.5)/((x-0.5)+(0.9-0.5)). x=0.90: 0.5; x=1.00: 0.5/0.9 = 0.5556. Node re-run, Demo.tsx mix().

claims.text: In the same game the kicker's scoring chance at the best mixes rises from 0.700 to 0.722.
In a mixed equilibrium each side's mix is set so the other side gains nothing from either of its choices.
claims.source: Easley & Kleinberg (2010), Networks, Crowds, and Markets, ch. 6 (mixed strategies and equilibrium; section 6.7 unconfirmed, proxy 403 when the brief was written). Needs the section checked against the free PDF.

claims.text: The lesson uses made-up numbers: it shows the logic, not real penalty rates.
claims.source: The payoffs 0.5, 0.9 and 0.9 to 1.0 are chosen for the toy game (brief). The empirical claim that real penalty data are close to the predicted mixes (Palacios-Huerta 2003, Review of Economic Studies 70(2)) is deliberately omitted: it was recalled from memory and needs a human source check before it could appear.

claims.text: In the toy game at 1.00, if the kicker keeps shooting left 50% of the time, a keeper who dives left every time holds him to 0.700 (a right dive would concede 0.750), the same scoring chance as at 0.90.
claims.source: Kicker at p=0.5: dive left gives 0.5*0.5+0.5*0.9 = 0.700; dive right gives 0.5*1.0+0.5*0.5 = 0.750. Keeper picks the lower, so 0.700 = the 0.90 value. Node re-run of Demo.tsx mix(100, true).

claims.text: In the toy game at 1.00 with both sides at their best mixes (kicker left 44.4%, keeper left 55.6%), either keeper dive concedes 0.722 and either kick scores 0.722.

recall.question: In a mixed-strategy game like the penalty kick, you improve one of your two moves. What happens to how often your best mix uses that move?
options: It can go down, because your opponent now guards it more
recall.why: Your mix is set to keep the other side indifferent. A stronger move makes them guard it more, so you use it less, yet you can score more overall.
